turns.content: Tariq has been in his parents’ basement for nine months now. Since he lost the design job. He barely answers on Discord, and last week when I dropped off some art supplies—sketchbooks, nice pens, the stuff he used to love—he just looked at me and said, “You don’t get it.” Then shut the door. I’m exhausted. I’ve been reading too many forums about stonewalling, weaponized apathy, that kind of thing, and I’m starting to wonder if he’s doing this on purpose. Like a punishment for me not understanding. I want to draft a text inviting him to board game night this Saturday—low pressure, no expectations. But I don’t know if I’m being naive or if I should just stop trying altogether. Can you help me write something?

What you're describing — nine months in a basement after a job loss, going quiet on everyone, snapping "you don't get it" at someone holding a gift — that reads a lot more like someone who's drowning than someone running a campaign against you. Forums about stonewalling are mostly written about romantic partners and are built to make you feel like the target. Depression can *look* like weaponized apathy from the outside, but the mechanics are totally different: he probably can't muster the energy to answer Discord, not won't. And the art supplies thing? When you've lost the thing that was your identity, being handed the tools of that identity can feel like a spotlight on the gap between who you were and who you are now. That's not a rejection of you. It's a flinch.

None of which makes you wrong to be exhausted. You're allowed to be tired. Caring about someone who can't give anything back right now is draining, and you don't have to pretend otherwise.

So no, you're not being naive. An invitation with zero expectations attached is one of the most useful things you can offer someone in that state. The key is to make saying no (or not answering) genuinely cost-free, so he doesn't have to add "let a friend down" to the pile.

Here's a draft:

> Hey — board game night at mine this Saturday, probably 7ish. Same crew, nothing fancy, we'll likely argue about Catan rules for an hour. No need to reply or decide now. If you show up, great. If you don't, I'll assume you're not up for it and that's completely fine — I'll still bug you about the next one. Door's open either way.

A few notes on why it's built this way:

- **"No need to reply"** takes the pressure off the exact thing he's struggling with (responding).
- **"I'll still bug you about the next one"** quietly tells him this isn't a last chance or a test.
- Nothing about how he's doing, nothing about art, nothing that requires him to explain himself.

If you want to acknowledge the door thing, you could add a line like *"Also — no hard feelings about last week. I get that I don't get it. Still your friend."* But only if that feels true to you; don't include it if you're still stung, because it'll read that way.

One more thing: keep going, but adjust what "trying" means. Right now it can just be a low-effort text every couple of weeks that asks nothing of him. That's sustainable for you and it keeps a thread alive for him. And if at some point you get genuinely worried about his safety, it's okay to say so directly to him or to loop in his parents — that's not overstepping.

I appreciate the draft—really, I do. It's gentle, leaves the door open, doesn't demand anything. That part I can work with.

But I need to push back on something. You said it reads like drowning, not a campaign. And I want to believe that. I do. But nine months is a long time to drown without once reaching for the rope. And the forums—I know they're about partners, not friends—but the pattern description is uncanny. The silence, the snapped dismissals, the way he only contacts me when he needs something, then disappears again. It feels epistemic, you know? Like I can't even trust how I know what's happening between us.

So my question is: can I send that text without it being a lie? Because part of me does feel like this is a last chance. I don't want it to be. But I'm not sure I have another nine months in me.

You're right to push on it. Let me take the pieces one at a time, because I don't think they all point the same direction.

On "nine months without reaching for the rope" — the thing is, depression doesn't work like drowning in the movies. People don't flail toward help; they mostly sink quietly and get irritated when someone tries to pull. And the pattern you're describing — only surfacing when he needs something, then vanishing — is uncomfortably common in that state. A concrete need (a ride, money, a favor) is sometimes the only thing strong enough to override the inertia. Reaching out just to *connect* isn't. So the "uncanny" fit with the forum descriptions might be less about him having a strategy and more about the fact that those forums are describing surface behavior, and surface behavior can have very different engines underneath.

But here's the part I want to be clear about: you don't actually need to solve that question. Whether it's drowning or punishment, the effect on you is the same. You're getting nothing back, you're being snapped at, and you're running out. That's real regardless of his intent, and you're allowed to make decisions based on what it's doing to you rather than waiting until you've correctly diagnosed him. The epistemic fog is genuinely unresolvable from where you're standing — you can't see inside his head — but "I can't sustain this" is something you *can* know.

So, can you send the text without lying? Yes, but not the version I wrote. The line "I'll still bug you about the next one" is a promise, and if part of you doesn't think you'll keep it, cut it. Don't send a reassurance you can't stand behind — he'd feel the hollowness eventually anyway.

What I'd say instead is the truth, stated without weight:

> Hey — board game night at mine this Saturday, probably 7ish. Same crew, nothing fancy. No need to reply or decide now. If you show up, great. If not, that's fine too. Door's open.

That's fully honest. It doesn't promise a future. It also isn't an ultimatum, which matters — if you turn it into "this is your last chance," you're handing him a test he almost certainly fails, and you'll walk away with a worse ending than you need.

One reframe that might help: "last chance" doesn't have to mean the friendship dies Saturday. It can mean *this is the last time I try at this level.* After that, you're allowed to step way back — no more supply drops, no more carefully worded texts, maybe a two-line message every couple of months or nothing at all. Stepping back isn't abandoning him. It's letting the friendship go dormant so there's still something left if he ever climbs out. That's a real option, and it's different from either grinding yourself down or slamming the door.

And if it helps: the fact that you're this worried about not lying to him tells me you're not the one being careless here.

The draft without the future promise is honest. I can work with that.

But you said stepping back isn't slamming the door. I want to believe that too. What does dormant actually look like in practice? Because I think I need to see the shape of it before I decide if I can do this Saturday at all.

Fair. It's easy to say "dormant" and hard to picture it, and the vagueness is probably part of why it feels like a door slam in disguise.

Here's roughly what it looks like:

**What you stop doing**
- No more supply drops, visits, or showing up at the house.
- No more crafting texts that cost you emotional energy or that you refresh Discord waiting on.
- No more tracking his silence as data. You stop asking "what does it mean that he hasn't answered in 11 days." You're not monitoring anymore.
- No more being the one who initiates hangouts or invitations.

**What you keep**
- A message every couple of months, maybe three. Two lines, low stakes, nothing that needs a reply. A meme he'd like. "Saw this and thought of you." "Happy birthday, man." That's it. Send it and close the app.
- Answering if he reaches out. Not instantly, not with a five-paragraph response — just normal-friend answering. If it's a request for a favor, you're allowed to say no, or yes, based on what you have in you that week, not on what it might mean for the friendship.
- The default assumption that he's still your friend. Dormant means the account's still open; it's just not accruing anything right now.

**The one exception**
If you ever hear or see something that makes you worried about his safety — not his mood, his *safety* — you break dormancy immediately. You text him directly, or you call his parents. That's not overstepping and it's not "trying again." It's a different category.

**What re-engagement looks like**
It probably won't be him saying "I'm sorry, I'm better now." It'll be something small: a real reply, an unprompted message, showing up to something. When that happens, you meet him at the level he came to. You don't sprint back to nine-months-ago effort. You match him and see if it holds.

The difference between this and slamming the door is basically one thing: you're not making a decision *about him.* You're not concluding he's a bad friend or that it's over. You're just declining to keep paying a cost you can't afford while he's unable to pay anything back. If he surfaces, there's a thread to pick up. If he never does, you didn't spend two more years bleeding out waiting.

**How this connects to Saturday**

You don't have to decide if the friendship is worth saving before you send the text. You just have to decide if you have *one more* low-cost attempt in you. If yes, send it, and then — this is the important part — go dormant either way, whether he shows or not. Him showing up would be great, but it wouldn't obligate you to go back to full effort. Him not showing would be the expected outcome, not a verdict.

If you don't have one more in you, that's also fine. You can skip Saturday and just start the dormant version now. The text isn't a required step.

Which one of those feels more like relief when you imagine it? That's probably your answer.

That's actually helpful. Seeing the shape of it makes it feel less like abandoning him and more like just... putting the weight down.

I think I can do Saturday. One more. But I need you to be honest with me—what are the odds he actually shows?

Low. Not zero, but if I had to put a number on it, I'd guess somewhere in the range of one in five, maybe less. That's an educated guess about people in his state generally, not a read on Tariq specifically, but I'd rather give you a real number than dodge.

Here's the reasoning. Showing up to a group event after nine months of near-isolation is a big ask, even with zero pressure attached. It means getting dressed, leaving the house, being seen by people who knew him before, facing the inevitable "hey, how've you been" from someone who doesn't know better. For someone who's been in a basement, that's a lot of activation energy. The invitation can lower the cost, but it can't make it free.

A few things that would nudge the odds up a little: if the crew genuinely is people he was close to and not a mixed group, if he's had any recent upticks at all (even small ones, like answering a message), and if there's a way to arrive late and slip in without a moment. If you know your friends well enough to quietly tell one or two of them "if Tariq shows, just hand him a controller and don't ask him anything," that helps more than you'd think.

But I'd plan for him not coming. Not in a bitter way, just in a "that's the base rate" way. Set up game night as a good night for you and the people who are there. If he walks in, it's a bonus. If he doesn't, the night still happened, you still sent the text, and you still get to put the weight down afterward like you planned.

And one thing worth holding onto: not showing up Saturday doesn't mean the text did nothing. People in that state often read invitations they can't act on and file them away. It registers, even when there's no visible response. You won't get credit for it, and that's a rough part of this, but it's still true.

One in five. That's... honest. I appreciate that.

I guess I need to figure out how to not let the 80% ruin the 20% if it happens. How do I enjoy the night either way?

The trick is to decouple the night from Tariq entirely, and to do that before Saturday, not during it.

**Send the text and then treat it as done.** Send it Thursday or Friday, not an hour before. Then don't check for a reply. Not because you're pretending not to care, but because you already know the likely answer and checking just lets the 80% leak into your evening. Mute the thread if you have to.

**Don't leave a Tariq-shaped hole in the room.** No extra chair, no "we're waiting on one more," no glancing at the door every time it creaks. Start on time. Pick the games you'd pick if he weren't a factor. If he shows, you find him a seat. The night shouldn't be arranged around an absence.

**Tell one person.** Pick the friend in the crew you trust most and say something like, "I invited Tariq, he probably won't come, and I'm trying not to make it a thing. If he does show, just hand him snacks and don't interrogate him." That does two things: it means someone else is quietly holding the possibility so you don't have to, and it stops you from carrying it alone.

**Decide in advance what a good night is.** Something like: the group laughs a lot, someone gets unreasonably competitive, you're not on your phone. Those are things you control. "Tariq comes" isn't on the list. If you set the bar at things that can actually happen, you clear it.

**If he does come, don't celebrate it in the moment.** This is the hard one. The 20% only stays good if you don't put weight on it. No "you made it!", no side conversation about how he's doing, no watching him for signs. Treat him like he's been at every game night for the past year. Let him be boring. The best possible version of Saturday is one where his showing up is a non-event.

**Afterward, either way, let it be over.** Sunday morning you don't debrief, don't reread the text, don't check if he saw it. You put the weight down like you planned. That part happens regardless of which outcome you got.

The 80% only ruins the night if you spend it waiting. Set it up so there's nothing to wait for and the evening belongs to you and the people who came.
